Consequently, the ‘constrained’ Hamiltonian $F$ defined by (2.9) boils down to the usual Hamiltonian for drift control

$$ \displaystyle F_{t}(x,y,z,S)=\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}}\big\{\sigma_{t}(x)\lambda_{t}(x,b)\cdot z-c_{t}(x,b)-k_{t}(x,b)y\big\},\;(t,x,y,z)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},\;S\in\Sigma_{t}(x), $$

and is thus independent of the $S$ -variable. It is straightforward to see that taking $\psi\equiv F$ in the general contract form introduced in Definition 3.2 allows to recover the above contract. This choice naturally satisfies Condition C ℛ , as well as Condition C min 𝒲 with minimum achieved for any $\gamma\in E$ . However, this natural choice does not satisfy Condition C sup 𝒲 , as the supremum of $\psi$ is clearly $F$ instead of $\infty$ . Nevertheless, the existing literature on principal–agent problems with drift control actually always assumes weak uniqueness for the controlled SDE (2.2). Therefore, the optimality of the contract form can be proved using the BSDE-approach as in Section 3.3.2 and, as highlighted before, the first part of Condition C sup 𝒲 is actually not needed for this approach. We emphasise that, without the assumption of weak uniqueness, the representation of the optimal contract would involve an additional term, namely an orthogonal martingale, and it remains unclear in general settings whether such a term can be taken to be zero without loss of generality. For further details on this technical point, we refer to [5, Remarks 2.3 and 3.3], as well as the general approach in Kršek and Possamaï (2026) [16].

In a framework with volatility control, and where Assumption 2.3 is satisfied, the approach introduced in [8] is valid, implying that the original contract form (2.11) is optimal. This form can be recovered from our more general form of contracts introduced in Definition 3.2 by taking

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big],\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}). $$

Indeed, one can first compute that, by definition of $H$ or directly using (2.10)

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\big\{\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\big\}=H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)-\sup_{S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big]\bigg\}=0, $$

thus Condition C ℛ is satisfied. Still using the definition of $H$ , we also have that for all $S^{\prime}\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$

$$ \displaystyle H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\geq F_{t}(x,y,z,S^{\prime})+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S^{\prime}\big], $$

so that provided that for any $(t,x,S)$ , we can always find $S^{\circ}_{t}(x)\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ such that $S^{\circ}_{t}(x)\prec S$ $($ or $S\prec S^{\circ}_{t}(x))$ , where $\prec$ is the standard—strict—partial order on the set of symmetric semi-definite, $d\times d$ matrices with real entries, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\geq F_{t}(x,y,z,S^{\prime})+\dfrac{1}{2}\sup_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\big\{{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma(S^{\prime}-S)\big]\big\}=+\infty. $$

Finally, under Assumption 2.3, there exists a Borel-measurable function $\gamma^{\star}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S),S)=H_{t}\big(x,y,z,\gamma^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)\big)-\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)S\big]=F_{t}(x,y,z,S). $$

From the two equations above, we conclude that $\psi$ also satisfies Conditions C min 𝒲 and C sup 𝒲 .

Our objective is now to construct an explicit function $\psi$ for the general case, so as to ensure the existence of an optimal contract when the volatility is controlled but Assumption 2.3 does not hold. In the following sections, we present two natural choices for $\psi$ , derived respectively from the ‘contractible-volatility’ and 2BSDE approaches.

### 4.2 Duality contracts

When Assumption 2.3 does not hold, one can slightly correct the original contract form (2.11) introduced in [8]. We have seen in the previous section that a natural choice for $\psi$ is (4.3), or equivalently in the form (4.1) with $\overline{\psi}$ defined as

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big],\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}). $$

This construction works under Assumption 2.3 since, in this case, $F$ coincides (abusing notations slightly) with its bi-conjugate $F^{\star\star}$ , defined for all $(t,x,y,z)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ by

$$ \displaystyle F^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)\coloneqq \displaystyle\ \inf_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\bigg\{H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big]\bigg\}. $$

While the above link breaks when Assumption 2.3 does not hold, the intuition is to define $\overline{\psi}$ with $F^{\star\star}$ introduced above instead of $F$ , which will then naturally coincide with its bi-conjugate, restoring duality.

With this in mind, we now specify the parametrisation function $\psi$ via (4.1), with $\overline{\psi}$ defined using $F^{\star\star}$ in (4.4) above

$$ \overline{\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq-F^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S],\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}). $$

Since $H$ is convex—as the convex conjugate of $(-2F)$ —it coincides with its bi-conjugate, and we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\bf\Sigma$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\overline{\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S^{\prime})=\inf_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\bf\Sigma$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{-\inf_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\bigg\{H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big]\bigg\}-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S^{\prime}]\bigg\}=-H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma), $$

for all $(t,x,y,z,\gamma,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S) \displaystyle=F_{t}(x,y,z,S)-F^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S]+H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma). $$

We are thus considering terminal payments of the form $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}(Y_{\text{$T$}})$ with

$$ \displaystyle Y_{\text{$T$}} \displaystyle=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}H_{s}(Y_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{s}\mathrm{d}[X]_{s}\big]+\int_{0}^{T}\big(F^{\star\star}-F\big)_{s}\big(Y_{s},Z_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s. $$

By construction of $\psi$ via (4.1), Condition C ℛ is naturally satisfied. Then, Lemma 4.1 also applies here using standard convex duality. However, if $H$ fails to be strictly convex in $\gamma$ , the infimum over $\gamma$ may not be attained. In this case, one may replace $H$ by any other strictly convex function, say $\overline{H}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)$ ,44 4 A natural choice here would be a quadratic perturbation of the form $\overline{H}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\coloneqq H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma\gamma^{\top}],\;\varepsilon>0$ . and take instead

$$ \overline{\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=-\inf_{\gamma^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\bigg\{\overline{H}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma^{\prime})-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma^{\prime}S]\bigg\}-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S]=-\overline{H}^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S]. $$

This leads to

$$ \psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\overline{H}^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\overline{H}^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}[\gamma S], $$

so that the infimum over $\gamma$ is still $0$ by Fenchel duality, but it is also attained by strict convexity. Finally, using the standard partial order on symmetric matrices, and assuming that for any $(t,x,S)$ , we can always find $S_{t}^{\circ}(x)\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ such that $S^{\circ}_{t}(x)\prec S$ $($ or $S\prec S_{t}^{\circ}(x))$ , we obtain the desired behaviour at infinity for $\psi$ . Under these assumptions, $\psi\in\Psi$ and the contract form (4.5) above is optimal.

To interpret the new form of contract (4.5), recall first that, by (3.16), $F_{t}(x,y,z,S)-F^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)\leq 0,$ with equality only if Assumption 2.3 is satisfied, so this term corresponds to an extra cost for the principal in the contract form (4.5) compared to the original contract form (2.11). The economic interpretation of this extra cost is as follows: in general, the only way the agent can always reach the value $F^{\star\star}$ when optimising is if he is allowed to randomise his controls, unless of course strong duality holds. Absent randomisation, the agent can only be guaranteed to reach the smaller value $F$ . Hence, to properly align the agent’s incentives, the principal must compensate him for this extra duality gap. More precisely, write first

$$ F^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)=\inf_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\sup_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\mathbf{\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{F_{t}(x,y,z,S^{\prime})+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\big[\gamma(S^{\prime}-S)\big]\bigg\}, $$

and formally consider a randomised version of the above: assume for simplicity that $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ is convex and compact (so that in particular the restriction of ${\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ to it is still a Polish space), let $\mathfrak{S}_{t}(x)$ and $\mathfrak{S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ be the sets of probability measures on $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ and ${\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ respectively, and define

$$ \displaystyle\overline{F}^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S) \displaystyle\coloneqq\inf_{\gamma\in\text{$\mathfrak{S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\sup_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\mathfrak{S}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\int_{\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\int_{\text{$\mathbf{\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{F_{t}(x,y,z,\mathrm{s})+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\big[g(S-\mathrm{s})\big]S^{\prime}(\mathrm{d}\mathrm{s})\gamma(\mathrm{d}g)\bigg\}. $$

The function on the right-hand side is clearly bilinear with respect to $(\gamma,S^{\prime})$ , and since $\mathfrak{S}_{t}(x)$ is convex and compact (for the weak topology) and $\mathfrak{S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ is convex, we can apply Sion’s minimax theorem to deduce

$$ \displaystyle\overline{F}^{\star\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S) \displaystyle\coloneqq\sup_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\mathfrak{S}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\inf_{\gamma\in\text{$\mathfrak{S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\int_{\text{$\mathbf{\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\int_{\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\bigg\{F_{t}(x,y,z,\mathrm{s})+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\big[g(S-\mathrm{s})\big]S^{\prime}(\mathrm{d}\mathrm{s})\gamma(\mathrm{d}g)\bigg\} \displaystyle=\inf_{\gamma\in\text{$\mathfrak{S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\int_{\text{$\mathbf{\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\gamma(\mathrm{d}g)=F_{t}(x,y,z,S). $$

Strong duality always holds in this case (see Buckdahn, Li, and Quincampoix (2014) [4, Equation (1.11)] for similar arguments).

### 4.3 Forcing contracts

Alternatively, the ‘contractible-volatility’ approach developed in [5] makes natural the consideration of ‘forcing’—or ‘penalisation’—contracts, in the sense that such contracts should strongly incentivise the agent to choose efforts in order to achieve an optimal quadratic variation from the principal’s point of view. With this in mind, we propose the following contracts $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}(Y_{\text{$T$}})$ , where $Y$ is solution to

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}F_{s}\big(Y_{s},Z_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{t}\|\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}-\Gamma_{s}\|^{2}\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\int_{0}^{t}\inf_{\text{$S$}\in\text{$\bf\Sigma$}_{\text{$s$}}}\big\|S-\Gamma_{s}\big\|^{2}\mathrm{d}s, $$

indexed by a pair of processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ , satisfying appropriate integrability conditions derived from Definition 3.1, and where $\|A\|^{2}={\rm Tr}[A^{\top}A]$ for any $A\in{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ . The contract form (4.6) coincides with the general form (3.4) under the specification that $E\coloneqq{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ and

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\|S-\gamma\|^{2}-\inf_{\text{$S$}^{\text{$\prime$}}\in\text{$\bf\Sigma$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\big\|S^{\prime}-\gamma\big\|^{2}, $$

for all $(t,x,y,z,\gamma,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ , or equivalently using (4.1), $\overline{\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq\|S-\gamma\|^{2}=\|S\|^{2}+\|\gamma\|^{2}-2\mathrm{Tr}[S\gamma^{\top}].$ First, it is clear by definition that $\psi$ satisfies Condition C ℛ . Moreover, if $\gamma\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ , then the infimum in Condition C ℛ is achieved for $S=\gamma$ . To verify Conditions C min 𝒲 and C sup 𝒲 , we notice that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\gamma\in{\cal S}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S) \displaystyle\geq F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\sup_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\Big\{\|S-\gamma\|^{2}-\|S^{\prime\prime}-\gamma\|^{2}\Big\} \displaystyle=F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\|S\|^{2}-\|S^{\prime\prime}\|^{2}+\sup_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\big\{2{\rm Tr}[(S^{\prime\prime}-S)^{\top}\gamma]\big\} \displaystyle\geq F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\|S\|^{2}-\|S^{\prime\prime}\|^{2}+2\sup_{c\in\mathbb{R}}\big\{c\|S^{\prime\prime}-S\|^{2}\big\}=+\infty, $$

where $S^{\prime\prime}\in{\bf\Sigma}_{{t}}(x)$ and $S^{\prime\prime}\neq S$ , as well as, for $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\gamma\in{\cal S}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\inf_{\gamma\in{\cal S}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\bigg\{\|S-\gamma\|^{2}-\inf_{S^{\text{$\prime$}}\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)}\big\|S^{\prime}-\gamma\big\|^{2}\bigg\}=F_{t}(x,y,z,S), $$

achieved again for $\gamma=S$ . Alternatively, one can check that this corresponds to $\eta$ -convexity in the sense of Lemma 4.1 with $\eta_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\coloneqq 2\mathrm{Tr}[S\gamma^{\top}]-\|\gamma\|^{2}$ and the choice $\ell(S)=\|S\|^{2}$ , which is $\eta$ -convex since

$$ \|S\|^{2}=\sup_{\gamma\in\text{${\cal S}$}_{\text{$d$}}(\mathbb{R})}\big\{-2\|\gamma\|^{2}-2\mathrm{Tr}[S\gamma^{\top}]+\|\gamma\|^{2}\big\}. $$

We highlight that this specification for $\psi$ also satisfies Condition 3.5, so the BSDE approach can be used to prove the optimality of this contract form.

The contract form (4.6) is quite natural when following the ‘contractible-volatility’ approach. Indeed, in the classical literature on contract theory, the usual technique to show that the first-best value can be achieved when the principal observes the agent’s control is to exhibit forcing contracts, namely contracts that strongly penalise the agent if his control deviates from the effort recommended by the principal. Applying this idea here, with the ‘observable’ control being the quadratic variation, naturally leads to the contract form (4.6), where the parameter $\Gamma$ chosen by the principal represents the density of the desired quadratic variation. More precisely, assuming to simplify that $\Gamma_{t}\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(X)$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ , then the contract can be simplified as follows

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}F_{s}\big(Y_{s},Z_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}-\int_{0}^{t}\|\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}-\Gamma_{s}\|^{2}\mathrm{d}s. $$

Comparing with the usual form of contract for drift control, the main difference is the last integral term, which is non-negative and thus clearly penalising the agent whenever the density $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}$ of the observable quadratic variation deviates from the recommended one announced by the principal via the parameter $\Gamma$ .

## 5 Examples and counter-examples

In this section, we revisit some of the examples and counter-examples introduced in the recent literature on principal–agent problems with volatility control. More precisely, in Section 5.1 we highlight that most application-related examples in the literature do in fact satisfy Assumption 2.3; see Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2017) [7], Aïd, Possamaï, and Touzi (2022) [1], and Baldacci and Possamaï (2022) [2] described below. In contrast, the following section recalls the counter-example proposed in [5, Section 4.3], where Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied, and hence the contract form (2.11) does not allow one to achieve the ‘contractible-volatility’ value, as demonstrated in [5]. We nevertheless show that the new contract form we propose attains this value. Finally, beyond the portfolio management example, [7] introduces a relatively general model—under CARA utility functions and within a Markovian framework—which was subsequently extended in [8]. However, despite additional convexity assumptions compared to [8], this more restrictive model may still fail to satisfy Assumption 2.3, as illustrated by a counter-example in Section 5.3.

### 5.1 Examples in the literature

We first recall several applied models from the literature and show that they satisfy Assumption 2.3, thereby confirming that the use of the original contract form (2.11) in these works is fully justified and that their results remain valid.

#### 5.1.1 Delegated portfolio management

In the example of [7, Section 2], the output process admits the following linear dynamics

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\big(v_{1}\beta^{1}_{t}+v_{2}\beta^{2}_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}t+\beta^{1}_{t}\mathrm{d}W^{1}_{t}+\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{d}W^{2}_{t},\;t\in[0,T], $$

where $\beta\coloneqq(\beta^{1},\beta^{2})$ denotes the agent’s control, taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $W^{1}$ and $W^{2}$ are two independent Brownian motions, and $(v_{1},v_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ are fixed parameters. The agent’s preferences are described by a CARA utility function and the following cost of effort, with constant parameters $(a_{1},a_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and $(k_{1},k_{2})\in(0,+\infty)^{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle k(b)=\dfrac{1}{2}k_{1}|b^{1}-a_{1}|^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}k_{2}|b^{2}-a_{2}|^{2},\;b\coloneqq(b^{1},b^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. $$

With this framework in mind, we are led to define for all $z\in\mathbb{R}$ and $b\coloneqq(b^{1},b^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$

$$ \displaystyle f(z,b)\coloneqq z(v_{1}b^{1}+v_{2}b^{2})-\dfrac{1}{2}k_{1}|b^{1}-a_{1}|^{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}^{k}_{2}|b^{2}-a_{2}|^{2}. $$

To introduce the agent’s ‘constrained’ Hamiltonian $F$ , we first note that the quadratic variation of $X$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}[X]_{t}=\big(|\beta_{t}^{1}|^{2}+|\beta_{t}^{2}|^{2}\big)\mathrm{d}t,\;t\in[0,T]. $$

In other words, for $S\in\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}$ describing the density of the quadratic variation fixed by the principal, the agent is constrained to choose his effort $\beta\coloneqq(\beta^{1},\beta^{2})$ taking values on the circle of radius $\sqrt{S}$ , characterised by

$$ g(S,b)\coloneqq|b^{1}|^{2}+|b^{2}|^{2}-S=0,\;\text{for}\;b\coloneqq(b^{1},b^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\;S\in\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}. $$

The agent’s ‘constrained’ Hamiltonian $F$ is thus defined for $(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}$ by

$$ \displaystyle F(z,S)\coloneqq\sup_{\{b\in\mathbb{R}^{\text{$2$}}:g(S,b)=0\}}\{f(z,b)\}. $$

To solve this constrained optimisation problem, we first introduce the corresponding Lagrangian

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(z,S,b,\lambda)\coloneqq f(z,b)-\lambda g(S,b),\;\text{for}\;(z,S,b,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}. $$

Computing the partial derivatives of $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to the variables $(b^{1},b^{2},\lambda)$ gives the following first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle zv_{1}-k_{1}(b^{1}-a_{1})-2\lambda b^{1}=0,\;zv_{2}-k_{2}(b^{2}-a_{2})-2\lambda b^{2}=0,\;|b^{1}|^{2}+|b^{2}|^{2}-S=0. $$

Solving the first two equations for $(b^{1},b^{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , we get

$$ b^{1,\star}(z,\lambda)=\dfrac{k_{1}a_{1}+zv_{1}}{k_{1}+2\lambda},\;b^{2,\star}(z,\lambda)=\dfrac{k_{2}a_{2}+zv_{2}}{k_{2}+2\lambda}. $$

To ensure that this point is a maximiser, one can compute the second-order condition and derive the admissible range for $\lambda$ , namely $\Lambda\coloneqq\big(-1/2\min\{k_{1},k_{2}\},+\infty\big).$ Now, plugging (5.2) in (5.1), we get

$$ \phi(z,\lambda)=S,\;\text{with}\;\phi(z,\lambda)\coloneqq\bigg|\dfrac{k_{1}a_{1}+zv_{1}}{k_{1}+2\lambda}\bigg|^{2}+\bigg|\dfrac{k_{2}a_{2}+zv_{2}}{k_{2}+2\lambda}\bigg|^{2},\;(z,\lambda,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}. $$

Differentiating $\phi(z,\lambda)$ with respect to $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\phi(z,\lambda)=-\frac{4|k_{1}a_{1}+zv_{1}|^{2}}{(k_{1}+2\lambda)^{3}}-\frac{4|k_{2}a_{2}+zv_{2}|^{2}}{(k_{2}+2\lambda)^{3}}. $$

Every denominator is strictly positive on $\Lambda$ ; hence $\phi(z,\lambda)$ is decreasing with respect to $\lambda\in\Lambda$ , with

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to\text{$-$}1/2\mathrm{min}\{k_{\text{$1$}},k_{\text{$2$}}\}}\phi(z,\lambda)=+\infty,\;\lim_{\lambda\to+\infty}\phi(z,\lambda)=0. $$

By continuity and strict monotonicity, we deduce that for fixed $(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}$ , there exists a unique solution $\lambda^{\star}(z,S)\in\Lambda$ to the implicit equation (5.3). The (unique) admissible optimal effort is thus given by

$$ \displaystyle b^{\star}(z,S)\coloneqq\big(b^{1,\star}(z,\lambda^{\star}(z,S)),\;b^{2,\star}(z,\lambda^{\star}(z,S))\big),\;(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}, $$

and the constrained Hamiltonian can be computed as $F(z,S)=f(z,b^{\star}(z,S))$ . To investigate the curvature of $F$ , note that the parameter $S$ appears inside $\mathcal{L}$ only linearly as $\lambda S$ , so the equality–constrained envelope theorem yields

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\text{$S$}}F(z,S)=\lambda^{\star}(z,S),\;\text{and}\;\partial_{\text{$S$}\text{$S$}}F(z,S)=\partial_{S}\lambda^{\star}(z,S)\;(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}. $$

To compute $\partial_{S}\lambda^{\star}$ , one can differentiate (5.3) to obtain $\partial_{\text{$S$}}\lambda^{\star}(z,S)=1/{\partial_{\lambda}\phi(z,\lambda)},\;(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}.$ By previous computation, $\partial_{\lambda}\phi$ is negative, implying that $\partial_{\text{$S$}\text{$S$}}F(z,S)\leq 0$ . This shows that $F$ is concave in $S$ .

#### 5.1.2 Green bonds investment

We now study the investment model introduced by Baldacci and Possamaï (2022) [2], which differs from the delegated portfolio management example in Section 5.1.1 in that it allows a control of arbitrary dimension $m$ and correlated Brownian motions. In this setting, the agent controls the output process through $\beta\coloneqq(\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{m})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} \displaystyle=(\beta_{t}^{\top}v)\mathrm{d}t+\beta_{t}^{\top}\mathrm{d}W_{t}, $$

where $v\coloneqq(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})$ denote the drift loadings and $W\coloneqq(W^{1},\dots,W^{m})$ is an $m$ -dimensional Brownian motion with $\mathrm{d}[W]_{t}=C\mathrm{d}t$ , for $C\in{\cal S}_{m}^{\text{$+$}}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $C_{ii}=1$ and $|C_{ij}|\leq 1$ . Using the notations from the previous section and the cost functions from [2], we define

$$ \displaystyle f(z,b)\coloneqq z\,v^{\top}b-\frac{1}{2}(b-a)^{\top}K(b-a),\;g(S,b)\coloneqq b^{\top}Cb-S,\;(z,S,b)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}, $$

where $a\coloneqq(a_{1},\dots,a_{m})$ are the cost targets, and $K\coloneqq\mathrm{diag}(k_{1},\dots,k_{m})\succ 0$ the cost weights. The first-order conditions from the associated Lagrangian yield

$$ \displaystyle zv-K(b-a)-2\lambda Cb=0\Longleftrightarrow(K+2\lambda C)b=Ka+zv. $$

Define $M(\lambda)\coloneqq K+2\lambda C$ and $r\coloneqq Ka+zv$ . Then $b^{\star}(z,\lambda)=M(\lambda)^{-1}r.$ To ensure $M(\lambda)\succ 0$ , set $G\coloneqq K^{-1/2}CK^{-1/2}\succ 0$ and let $\kappa_{\rm max}$ be the largest eigenvalue of $G$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle M(\lambda)\succ 0\Longleftrightarrow K^{-1/2}M(\lambda)K^{-1/2}=\mathrm{I}+2\lambda G\succ 0\Longleftrightarrow 1+2\lambda\kappa_{i}>0,\;\forall i\in\{1,\dots,m\}\Longleftrightarrow\lambda>-\frac{1}{2\kappa_{\text{$\rm max$}}}. $$

Hence $M(\lambda)\succ 0$ if and only if $\lambda\in\Lambda\coloneqq\big(-1/(2\kappa_{\rm max}),\infty\big)$ . Define $\phi(z,\lambda)\coloneqq b^{\star\top}C\,b^{\star}=r^{\top}M(\lambda)^{-1}C\,M(\lambda)^{-1}r,$ and diagonalise $G$ . Since $M(\lambda)=K^{1/2}(\mathrm{I}+2\lambda G)K^{1/2}$ , we get $M(\lambda)^{-1}=K^{-1/2}(\mathrm{I}+2\lambda G)^{-1}K^{-1/2}$ . Let $G=UDU^{\top}$ with $U$ orthonormal and $D=\mathrm{diag}(\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{m})$ . Set $q\coloneqq K^{-1/2}r$ , $\hat{q}\coloneqq U^{\top}q$ . Then for $\lambda\in\Lambda$

$$ \displaystyle\phi(z,\lambda)=q^{\top}(\mathrm{I}+2\lambda G)^{-1}G(\mathrm{I}+2\lambda G)^{-1}q=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\kappa_{i}}{(1+2\lambda\kappa_{i})^{2}}\,\hat{q}_{i}^{2},\text{ and }\;\partial_{\lambda}\phi(z,\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(-\frac{4\kappa_{i}^{2}}{(1+2\lambda\kappa_{i})^{3}}\right)\hat{q}_{i}^{2}, $$

hence $\phi$ is decreasing with respect to $\lambda$ on its domain. Moreover, since $\kappa_{i}/(1+2\lambda\kappa_{i})^{2}\longrightarrow 0$ as $\lambda\longrightarrow+\infty$ and $\kappa_{\rm max}/(1+2\lambda\kappa_{\rm max})^{2}\longrightarrow+\infty$ when $\lambda\downarrow-1/(2\kappa_{\rm max})$ , we deduce the following limits

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\to+\infty}\phi(z,\lambda)=0,\;\text{and}\;\lim_{\lambda\downarrow-1/(2\kappa_{\text{$\rm max$}}}\phi(z,\lambda)=+\infty. $$

Since $\phi(z,\lambda)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on $\Lambda$ , for any $S>0$ there is a unique solution $\lambda^{\star}(z,S)$ to $\phi(z,\lambda)=S$ . Following the same steps as in the delegated portfolio case, we conclude that $F$ is concave in $S$ , verifying Assumption 2.3.

#### 5.1.3 Demand–response programs in electricity markets

We conclude this section with the study of the demand–response model introduced by Aïd, Possamaï, and Touzi (2022) [1]. In this model, the dynamics of the (one-dimensional) output process is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(-\alpha^{i}_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{i}\sqrt{\beta^{i}_{t}}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{i}\Big),\;t\in[0,T], $$

with $W\coloneqq(W^{1},\dots,W^{n})$ a $n$ -dimensional Brownian motion and $(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n})\in\big(\mathbb{R}^{\star}_{+}\big)^{n}$ , and is controlled by the agent through the pair of processes $(\alpha,\beta)$ , taking values in $A\coloneqq[0,\bar{a}]^{n}$ and $B\coloneqq(0,1]^{n}$ respectively, with $\bar{a}>0$ . The agent’s cost of effort on the drift and volatility are respectively denoted by $c_{1}(a)$ for $a\in A$ and $c_{2}(b)$ for $b\in B$ ; in particular

$$ \displaystyle c_{2}(b)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{k_{i}}\big(b_{i}^{-1}-1\big),\;b\coloneqq(b_{1},\dots,b_{n})\in(0,1]^{n},\;(k_{1},\dots,k_{n})\in\big(\mathbb{R}^{\star}_{+}\big)^{n}. $$

We first note that $x\longmapsto x^{-1}$ is strictly convex on $(0,1]$ , so $c_{2}$ is convex on $B$ . For later use, we define the maximal attainable radius $S_{\mathrm{max}}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}$ , and let for $S\in(0,S_{\max}]$

$$ \displaystyle m(S)\coloneqq\inf_{\{b\in\text{$B$}:|\sigma(b)|^{\text{$2$}}=\text{$S$}\}}c_{2}(b),\;\text{with}\;|\sigma(b)|^{2}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}b_{i},\;b\coloneqq(b_{1},\dots,b_{n})\in(0,1]^{n}. $$

Taking into account the agent’s utility of consumption $u(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , the agent’s ‘constrained’ Hamiltonian is

$$ \displaystyle F(x,z,S)=u(x)-\inf_{a\in\text{$A$}}\big\{a\cdot\mathbf{1}_{n}z+c_{1}(a)\big\}-\frac{1}{2}m(S),\;(x,z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times(0,S_{\max}]. $$

We verify below that the mapping $S\longmapsto m(S)$ is convex on $(0,S_{\max}]$ , and consequently, $S\longmapsto F(S)$ is concave on the same interval, as required. For any $(S_{1},S_{2})\in(0,S_{\max}]^{2}$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$ , define $S_{\theta}\coloneqq\theta S_{1}+(1-\theta)S_{2}$ . First, compactness of $B$ and continuity of $|\sigma(\cdot)|^{2}$ ensure the existence of $b^{(i)}\in B$ such that $|\sigma(b^{(i)})|^{2}=S_{i}$ and $c_{2}(b^{(i)})=m(S_{i})$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ . Define then $b^{(\theta)}\coloneqq\theta b^{(1)}+(1-\theta)b^{(2)}\in B$ . Because $|\sigma(\cdot)|^{2}$ is affine in $b$

$$ \displaystyle\big|\sigma\big(b^{(\theta)}\big)\big|^{2}=\theta\big|\sigma\big(b^{(1)}\big)\big|^{2}+(1-\theta)\big|\sigma\big(b^{(2)}\big)\big|^{2}=S_{\theta}. $$

In other words, $b^{(\theta)}\in B$ satisfies the constraint $|\sigma(b^{(\theta)})|^{2}=S_{\theta}$ . Finally, applying convexity of $c_{2}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle m(S_{\theta})\leq c_{2}\big(b^{(\theta)}\big)\leq\theta c_{2}\big(b^{(1)}\big)+(1-\theta)c_{2}\big(b^{(2)}\big)=\theta m(S_{1})+(1-\theta)m(S_{2}). $$

The inequality above proves that $m$ is convex, implying that $F$ is concave in the $S$ -variable and Assumption 2.3 holds.

### 5.2 Duality gap

In the three models considered above, Assumption 2.3 holds, ensuring that the original contract form (2.11) is optimal and that the results of these papers remain valid. To the best of our knowledge, other applications of principal–agent problems with volatility control rely on closely related frameworks, as in Élie, Hubert, Mastrolia, and Possamaï (2021) [10] which extends [1] with the same form of dynamics and costs: a similar reasoning shows that Assumption 2.3 still holds there. While we cannot claim that every applied model necessarily satisfies Assumption 2.3, all those we are aware of actually do. Nevertheless, the assumption is not automatic: beyond usual specifications, one can construct reasonable counter-examples where it fails, as highlighted in [5, Section 4.3]. Nevertheless, we show here that the new contract form we propose allows to achieve this value.

We start by briefly recalling the framework introduced in [5, Section 4.3]. The controlled state equation is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}}_{t},\;t\in[0,T],\;X_{0}=0, $$

where $W$ is a one-dimensional Brownian motion and the agent’s control process $\beta$ can only take values in $[-1,1]$ . The agent’s objective function to be maximised over admissible probability measures $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\xi-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}c(\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{t})\mathrm{d}t\bigg],\;c(b)=1-b^{4},\;b\in[-1,1]. $$

The principal’s criteria is then defined as follows

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[X_{T}-\xi-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(\Sigma_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}t\bigg],\;c_{\text{$\rm P$}}(S)\coloneqq S^{3},\;S\in[0,1]. $$

In both criteria, we make explicit the dependence in the density $\Sigma$ of the quadratic variation $[X]$ , in order to study both the original problem, in which $\Sigma$ is controlled by the agent through his choice of $\beta$ , and its ‘contractible-volatility’ reformulation, in which the principal controls $\Sigma$ thus forcing the agent to choose his control $\beta$ so that $\beta^{2}=\Sigma$ .

#### ‘Contractible-volatility’ case.

It is shown in [5] that when the principal directly controls the density $\Sigma$ of the quadratic variation, she can reach the maximum value of $-R_{\text{$\rm A$}}-23T/27$ . More precisely, in the ‘contractible-volatility’ formulation, we know that the following contract form is optimal

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}F(\Sigma_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}, $$

where the pair of processes $(Z,\Sigma)$ has to be chosen by the principal, and for all $S\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle F(S)\coloneqq\sup_{\{b\in[\text{$-$}1,1]:b^{\text{$2$}}=\text{$S$}\}}\big\{-c(b)\big\}=\sup_{\{b\in[\text{$-$}1,1]:b^{\text{$2$}}=\text{$S$}\}}\big\{b^{4}-1\big\}=S^{2}-1,\;\text{for}\;b^{\circ}(S)=\pm\sqrt{S}. $$

Note that since the constrained Hamiltonian $F$ is convex—not concave—Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied. The agent’s optimal efforts are given by the maximisers of $F$ , here $\beta_{\cdot}^{\circ}=\pm\sqrt{\Sigma_{\cdot}}$ , which leads to $F(\Sigma_{\cdot})=\Sigma_{\cdot}^{2}-1$ . Finally, one can optimise the principal’s criteria defined by (5.5) by choosing $\Sigma\equiv 2/3$ , since by pointwise optimisation

$$ \displaystyle V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm P$}}=-y_{0}-T\bigg(1-\max_{\text{$S$}\in[0,1]}\big\{S^{2}-S^{3}\big\}\bigg)=-y_{0}-23T/27. $$

Maximising this value over $y_{0}$ under the agent’s participation constraint naturally leads to the choice $y_{0}=R_{\text{$\rm A$}}$ .

#### Duality gap.

It is shown in [5] that, when restricting to contracts of the form (2.11) in the original formulation of the principal–agent problem—when $\Sigma$ is not directly controlled by the principal—, the ‘contractible-volatility’ value previously computed cannot be reached. More precisely, one can first compute that for $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \displaystyle H(\gamma) \displaystyle\coloneqq\sup_{b\in[-1,1]}\bigg\{\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma b^{2}-c(b)\bigg\}=\begin{cases}\gamma/2,\;\mbox{if}\;\gamma>-2,\;\text{for}\;b^{\star}(\gamma)\in\{-1,1\},\\
-1,\;\mbox{if}\;\gamma=-2,\;\text{for}\;b^{\star}(\gamma)\in\{-1,0,1\},\\
-1,\;\mbox{if}\;\gamma<-2,\;\text{for}\;b^{\star}(\gamma)=0.\end{cases} $$

Then, using the form of contract (2.11) in the principal’s criteria (5.5), where here the density of the quadratic variation is determined through the agent’s optimal response to the contract, namely $\Sigma^{\star}_{\cdot}=|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{\cdot})|^{2}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(\xi,\Sigma^{\star},\mathbb{P}^{\star}\big)=-y_{0}+\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\bigg(H(\Gamma_{t})-\dfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{t}|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}\big)\bigg)\mathrm{d}t\bigg], $$

where now $\Gamma$ has to be chosen optimally. Again by pointwise optimisation, we compute that for $c_{\text{$\rm P$}}(S)=S^{3}$ , $S\in[0,1]$

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{H(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma|b^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|b^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}\big)\bigg\}=-1,\;\text{for}\;\gamma^{\star}=-2, $$

leading to a value of $-R_{\text{$\rm A$}}-T$ , (strictly) lower than the one previously obtained in the ‘contractible-volatility’ case.

#### Reaching the ‘contractible-volatility’ value.

We show now that by relying on the more general class of contracts (3.4) introduced in this note, the ‘contractible-volatility’ value can indeed be reached, as theoretically proved in Section 3.3.2. For this, one can use for instance the contract form (4.6), which becomes in this specific example

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}F\big(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\big|\widetilde{\Gamma}_{t}-\Gamma_{t}\big|^{2}\mathrm{d}t-\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\big|\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}-\Gamma_{t}\big|^{2}\mathrm{d}t, $$

where $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{t}\coloneqq(\Gamma_{t}\vee 0)\wedge 1$ , for a control process $\Gamma$ chosen by the principal. Given this contract, the optimal action for the agent is given by the maximiser over $b\in[-1,1]$ of

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{F}(\gamma,b) \displaystyle\coloneqq-c(b)-F\big(b^{2}\big)-\dfrac{1}{2}\big|b^{2}-\gamma\big|^{2},\;\text{with}\;F(S)=S^{2}-1,\;S\in[0,1]. $$

This gives

$$ \displaystyle\max_{b\in[-1,1]}\widehat{F}(\gamma,b)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\min_{b\in[-1,1]}\big|b^{2}-\gamma\big|^{2}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\big|(\gamma\vee 0)\wedge 1-\gamma\big|^{2},\;\text{for}\;b^{\star}(\gamma)=\pm\sqrt{(\gamma\vee 0)\wedge 1}. $$

Therefore, under the agent’s optimal response, we have $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=|b^{\star}(\Gamma)|^{2}=\widetilde{\Gamma}$ , and the contract becomes

$$ \displaystyle\xi \displaystyle=y_{0}+T-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{4}\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}. $$

Hence, we can compute the principal’s objective under the agent’s best response,

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi,\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\mathbb{P}^{\star}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}\bigg[X_{T}-\xi-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}c_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t})\mathrm{d}t\bigg]=-y_{0}-T+\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\Big(|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{4}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|b^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}\big)\Big)\mathrm{d}t\bigg], $$

assuming sufficient integrability condition. Recalling that $c_{\text{$\rm P$}}(S)=S^{3}$ , by pointwise optimisation we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\Big\{|b^{\star}(\gamma)|^{4}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|b^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}\big)\Big\}=\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\Big\{|(\gamma\vee 0)\wedge 1|^{2}-|(\gamma\vee 0)\wedge 1|^{3}\Big\}=\max_{\gamma\in[0,1]}\{\gamma^{2}-\gamma^{3}\}=\dfrac{4}{27},\;\text{for}\;\gamma^{\star}=\dfrac{2}{3}. $$

We thus conclude that the new contract form (4.6) allows the principal to achieve her value in the reformulated problem. To achieve the ‘contractible-volatility’ value, one can also use the contract form (4.5). For this, we compute

$$ \displaystyle F^{\star\star}(S)\coloneqq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{H(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\}=S-1,\;\text{for}\;\gamma^{\star}=-2. $$

Note that this confirms that Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied here. Indeed, $F^{\star\star}(S)-F_{\text{$\rm A$}}(S)=S-S^{2}$ , which is (strictly) positive on $(0,1)$ , and equal to $0$ only if $S\in\{0,1\}$ . Therefore, $F^{\star\star}(S)\neq F(S)$ for all $S\in(0,1)$ . Considering the contract form (4.5), we obtain here

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\bigg(H(\Gamma_{t})+\big|\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big|^{2}-\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}-\dfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{t}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\bigg)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}. $$

Plugging this form into the agent’s expected utility, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\mathbb{P})=y_{0}+\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\bigg(|\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s}|^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{s}|\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s}|^{2}-1-H(\Gamma_{s})\bigg)\mathrm{d}s\bigg], $$

and therefore the optimal effort is obtained by computing

$$ \displaystyle\max_{b\in[-1,1]}\bigg\{|b|^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma|b|^{2}\bigg\} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}1+\gamma/2,\;\mbox{if}\;\gamma>-2,\;\text{for}\;\widetilde{b}(\gamma)\in\{-1,1\},\\
0,\;\mbox{if}\;\gamma=-2,\;\text{for}\;\widetilde{b}(\gamma)\in[-1,1],\\
0,\;\mbox{ if}\;\gamma<-2,\;\text{for}\;\widetilde{b}(\gamma)=0.\end{cases} $$

Looking at the principal’s problem defined by (5.5) when using contracts of the form (4.5), we have

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(\xi,\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\mathbb{P}^{\star}\big) \displaystyle=-y_{0}+\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\bigg(H(\Gamma_{t})+|\widetilde{b}(\Gamma_{t})|^{4}-|\widetilde{b}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{t}|\widetilde{b}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|\widetilde{b}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}\big)\bigg)\mathrm{d}t\bigg], $$

where $\Gamma$ has to be chosen optimally. Again by pointwise optimisation, we obtain for $c_{\text{$\rm P$}}(S)=S^{3}$

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{t}^{\star}\in\argmax_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{H(\gamma)+|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{4}-|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{2}-c_{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{2}\big)\bigg\}\equiv-2,\;t\in[0,T]. $$

Indeed, such a choice of $\gamma=-2$ makes the agent indifferent between any effort taking value in $[-1,1]$ , and gives a value of $-y_{0}-T(1+|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{4}-|\widetilde{b}(\gamma)|^{6})$ for the principal. She can then maximise this value by choosing among agent’s best response $\widetilde{b}(\gamma)\in\{-\sqrt{2/3},\sqrt{2/3}\}$ , and thus achieve her ‘contractible-volatility’ value.

### 5.3 Another counter-example

In this subsection, we exhibit a counter-example within the framework of [7, Section 3]. In particular, despite additional convexity assumptions compared to [8], this more restrictive model may still fail to satisfy Assumption 2.3. Let $(\alpha,\beta)$ be the agent’s effort taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and consider the following dynamics for the output process

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}(\alpha^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t}),\;t\in[0,T], $$

for $W$ a one-dimensional Brownian motion. The agent’s cost of effort is further defined as $k(a,b)=k_{1}|b|+k_{2}a^{2}$ for $(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and fixed constants $k_{1}>0$ and $k_{2}>0$ . Note that the above specification satisfies the conditions required in [7, Section 3]: the cost function $k$ is non-negative and convex and the linear growth condition [7, Equation (6)] holds since for every $(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $|a|+|b|\leq\ C(1+|a|+|b|)$ for all $C\geq 1$ .

Within this framework, the agent’s constrained Hamiltonian can be defined for $(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}$ as

$$ \displaystyle F(z,S) \displaystyle\coloneqq\sup_{\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{\text{$2$}}:b^{\text{$2$}}=\text{$S$}\}}\big\{zab-k_{1}|b|-k_{2}a^{2}\big\}=\sup_{\{b\in\mathbb{R}:b^{\text{$2$}}=\text{$S$}\}}\bigg\{-k_{1}|b|+\sup_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\big\{zab-k_{2}a^{2}\big\}\bigg\}. $$

Standard computations give

$$ \displaystyle F(z,S)=-k_{1}\sqrt{S}+\dfrac{z^{2}S}{4k_{2}},\;\text{with corresponding efforts}\;b^{\star}(z,S)\coloneqq\pm\sqrt{S},\;a^{\star}(z,S)\coloneqq\dfrac{zb^{\star}(z,S)}{2k_{2}},\;(z,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}. $$

Differentiating $F$ with respect to $S>0$ , we obtain for all $z\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\text{$S$}}F(z,S)=\frac{z^{2}}{4k_{2}}-\frac{k_{1}}{2\sqrt{S}},\;\partial_{\text{$S$}\text{$S$}}F(z,S)=\frac{k_{1}}{4S^{3/2}}. $$

Recalling that $k_{1}$ is a positive constant, the second derivative is positive for all $S>0$ . In other words, $F$ is strictly convex with respect to the $S$ -variable on $(0,\infty)$ , implying that Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied in this context.

With this in mind, letting $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ , we can use Itô’s formula to compute

$$ \displaystyle{\cal K}_{\text{$T$}}^{\mathbb{P}}Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi} \displaystyle=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\cal K}_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\Big(\psi_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)+k_{s}\big(\beta_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)Y_{s}-Z_{s}\cdot\mu_{s}(\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s})\Big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\cal K}_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}Z_{s}\cdot\sigma_{s}(\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s})\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}}_{s}. $$

Plugging this into the agent’s utility defined in (2.3) and using the integrability conditions on $Z$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}) \displaystyle=y_{0}+\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\cal K}_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\Big(f_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{s},Z_{s},\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s}\big)-\psi_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\Big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg], $$

recalling that $f$ is defined in (2.9). Using Condition C ℛ and the definition of $F$ in (2.9), we notice that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}}\big\{f_{t}(x,y,z,b)-\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\big\}=\sup_{\text{$S$}\in\text{${\bf\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}_{\text{$t$}}(x,\text{$S$})}\big\{f_{t}(x,y,z,b)\big\}-\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)\bigg\}=0, $$

for all $(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E$ , implying both that $J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P})\leq y_{0}$ for all $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ and $V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi)=y_{0}$ .

It remains to show that there exists (at least) an optimal response for the agent to $\xi$ . This can be deduced from (3.5) in Definition 3.1, which states that there is $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)=F_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)=f_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi},Z_{t},\beta^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}_{t}\big),\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\star}\text{\rm--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega, $$

implying both the existence of a process $\mathfrak{S}^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}\coloneqq S^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{\cdot},Z_{\cdot},\Gamma_{\cdot})$ , where $S^{\star,\psi}$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle S^{\star,\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\in\argmin_{\text{$S$}\in\text{${\bf\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\big\{\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\big\},\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E, $$

and of a process $\mathfrak{b}^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}\coloneqq b^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{\cdot},Z_{\cdot},\Gamma_{\cdot})$ , with $b^{\star,\psi}$ defined by (3.6). Hence $J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P})\leq y_{0}$ for all $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ , with $J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P})=y_{0}$ if and only if the agent’s effort is set to $\mathfrak{b}^{\star}_{t}=b^{\star}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})$ , $\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}$ –a.e., where $b^{\star}$ satisfies (3.6). ∎
